description: I am an electrical engineering student who loves to inspire curiosity and lead the youth (or anyone) to finding those aha moments along their learning journey. I am a solo team.
summary: Solar Storm Replay is a free browser game where players plan a lunar outpost and keep a crew of 4 alive for 30 days while finishing three real science goals: collecting soil samples, mapping ice and minerals, and running a radiation biology experiment. The twist: every mission secretly replays a real solar storm from NASA’s DONKI space weather database. When a flare alert arrives, players must decide whether to shelter (safe, but no science) or keep working and risk radiation. They also learn that a flare’s size doesn’t predict the particle danger. A live daily budget shows exactly how power, oxygen, water and food add up, so the trade-offs are visible, not hidden math. Playing the three landing sites makes it clear why NASA’s Artemis program is aiming for the lunar south pole: near-constant sunlight and water ice. The debrief reveals the real storm, compares real NASA dose rates on the ISS and the Moon to show how Earth’s magnetic field protects us, and puts space radiation on a real scale, from a chest X-ray to NASA’s 600 mSv career limit. It’s built for ages 7 to 12 in plain language, and anyone curious can play.
details:
What it does and how it works
Solar Storm Replay: Moonbase Mission Trainer is a free browser game where players plan a lunar outpost and guide a crew of 4 astronauts through a 30-day mission. It has three stages:

  1. Land: choose the south pole ridge (near-constant sunlight and water ice, but Earth sits low in the sky), the equatorial plains (two-week lunar night, no ice), or a lava-tube cave (natural radiation shield, but long nights).
  2. Build: spend a 100-unit launch mass budget on solar panels, a fission reactor, batteries, regolith shielding, an ice miner, a greenhouse, an oxygen generator, supply crates and a comms relay dish. A live daily budget shows how much power is made by day and by night, what each machine uses, and on which day oxygen, water or food would run out. Players see the trade-offs instead of doing the math in their heads.
  3. Survive and do science: each day, players choose indoor experiments, a moonwalk, maintenance, rest or the storm shelter. Every choice shows its radiation dose, science gain, power cost and effect on morale. To win, the crew must survive and finish three science goals based on real lunar science: collect soil samples, map ice and minerals, and run a radiation biology experiment. Two bonus goals, a moonquake network and growing plants in moon soil, reward players who push further at the cost of more radiation.

The core twist: every mission secretly replays a real solar storm from NASA’s DONKI space weather database. The storms are September 2017 (X9.3 and X8.2 flares, ending in Ground Level Enhancement 72), October 2021 (an X1.0 flare that caused GLE 73), May 2024 (X5.8 and X8.7 flares and Earth’s strongest geomagnetic storm since 2003), and the quiet solar minimum of December 2019. When a flare alert arrives, players decide whether to shelter (safe, but no science) or keep working and risk radiation. Without a comms dish, they can’t know whether dangerous particles are coming. With one, Earth’s forecasters warn them, but the dish costs mass that could have been supplies. Players learn something real forecasters deal with: a flare’s size doesn’t predict the particle danger.

After the mission, the debrief reveals which storm the player lived through, with the real DONKI record for each flare and the choice they made. It then compares radiation on Earth’s surface, on the ISS (real dose rates from NASA’s OSDR RadLab database) and on the Moon (LRO/CRaTER), to show how Earth’s magnetic field and atmosphere protect us and why lunar crews need storm shelters. A chart puts space radiation on a real scale, from a chest X-ray (0.1 mSv) to NASA’s 600 mSv career limit.

Benefits and intended impact
Space radiation is invisible and widely misunderstood. Many people fear radiation from nuclear power on Earth, but few know what solar storms mean for astronauts, or how much Earth’s magnetic field protects all of us. The game turns that into a decision players feel: a choice that saves science today can cost radiation tomorrow, and no option is free. Playing the different landing sites also shows why NASA’s Artemis program is aiming for the lunar south pole. It’s written in plain language for ages 7 to 12, with in-context explanations of terms like “ionizing” and “flare class,” and it works for older students, parents and classrooms too. A teacher mode lets a class replay the same storm and compare strategies. Since each run replays a different real storm, players learn from failure and try new plans.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page, with no download, account or install, so it runs on any laptop or tablet browser. The NASA data is archived and built into the game, and labeled as archived rather than live. The in-game radiation meter uses simplified units (a “mission radiation budget”), while the comparison chart uses real numbers from NASA-STD-3001, NASA and the National Academies. The slide deck was made in Claude’s slide editor, and screenshots were captured with Playwright. Claude (an AI model by Anthropic) helped write the code and text, gather and summarize the data sources, and build the deck. This is disclosed in the game and on the final slide.

What makes it creative
Most space games use invented numbers. This one replays real space weather history, so every playthrough is a real event, revealed at the end like a mystery. It doesn’t just say “radiation is dangerous.” It makes uncertainty part of the game: players often have to decide before they know how bad a storm will be, just as mission planners do.

Factors I considered

  • Keeping the number of systems manageable for young players.
  • Making sure no choice is free.
  • Showing per-day numbers so the trade-offs are visible, not hidden math.
  • Being honest about which data is real and which is simplified for gameplay.
  • Avoiding any NASA logos or branding.
  • Making failure a learning moment with a clear debrief, not a punishment.
